claim: Checkpoint inhibitor therapy of cancer has led to markedly improved survival of a subset of patients in multiple solid malignant tumor types.
source: Checkpoint inhibitor therapy of cancer has led to markedly improved survival of a subset of patients in multiple solid malignant tumor types, yet the factors driving these clinical responses or lack thereof are not known.
evidence: This claim is supported by references to established clinical outcomes in the field of checkpoint inhibitor therapy.

claim: The factors driving clinical responses or lack thereof to checkpoint inhibitor therapy are not known.
source: Checkpoint inhibitor therapy of cancer has led to markedly improved survival of a subset of patients in multiple solid malignant tumor types, yet the factors driving these clinical responses or lack thereof are not known.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: A mechanistic mathematical model has been developed for better understanding factors related to checkpoint inhibitor treatment outcome and optimizing personal treatment strategies.
source: We have developed a mechanistic mathematical model for better understanding these factors and their relations in order to predict treatment outcome and optimize personal treatment strategies.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the work performed in this study.

claim: The translational mathematical model is dependent on three key parameters: tumor growth rate (α), tumor-immune infiltration (Λ), and immunotherapy-mediated amplification of anti-tumor response (µ).
source: Here, we present a translational mathematical model dependent on three key parameters for describing efficacy of checkpoint inhibitors in human cancer: tumor growth rate (α), tumor-immune infiltration (Λ), and immunotherapy-mediated amplification of anti-tumor response (µ).
evidence: This describes the structure of the mathematical model developed in the study.

claim: The model was calibrated by fitting it to a compiled clinical tumor response dataset of 189 patients obtained from published anti-PD-1 and anti-PD-L1 clinical trials.
source: The model was calibrated by fitting it to a compiled clinical tumor response dataset (n = 189 patients) obtained from published anti-PD-1 and anti-PD-L1 clinical trials, and then validated on an additional validation cohort (n = 64 patients) obtained from our in-house clinical trials.
evidence: This describes the methodology used to calibrate the model with clinical data.

claim: The model was validated on an additional validation cohort of 64 patients obtained from in-house clinical trials.
source: The model was calibrated by fitting it to a compiled clinical tumor response dataset (n = 189 patients) obtained from published anti-PD-1 and anti-PD-L1 clinical trials, and then validated on an additional validation cohort (n = 64 patients) obtained from our in-house clinical trials.
evidence: This describes the validation methodology using independent clinical data.

claim: The derived parameters Λ and µ were both significantly different between responding versus nonresponding patients.
source: The derived parameters Λ and µ were both significantly different between responding versus nonresponding patients.
evidence: This is a statement of the statistical results from the model fitting.

claim: The model appropriately classified response in 81.4% of patients by using only tumor volume measurements and within 2 months of treatment initiation in a retrospective analysis.
source: Of note, our model appropriately classified response in 81.4% of patients by using only tumor volume measurements and within 2 months of treatment initiation in a retrospective analysis.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the retrospective analysis of the model's predictive performance.

claim: The model reliably predicted clinical response to the PD-1/PD-L1 class of checkpoint inhibitors across multiple solid malignant tumor types.
source: The model reliably predicted clinical response to the PD-1/PD-L1 class of checkpoint inhibitors across multiple solid malignant tumor types.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the model's performance across different cancer types.

claim: Comparison of model parameters to immunohistochemical measurement of PD-L1 and CD8+ T cells confirmed robust relationships between model parameters and their underlying biology.
source: Comparison of model parameters to immunohistochemical measurement of PD-L1 and CD8+ T cells confirmed robust relationships between model parameters and their underlying biology.
evidence: This describes validation of the model parameters against biological measurements.

claim: Model parameters may be informed directly from biopsy samples, which are conveniently obtainable as early as the start of treatment.
source: These results have demonstrated reliable methods to inform model parameters directly from biopsy samples, which are conveniently obtainable as early as the start of treatment.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the validation results showing model parameters can be derived from biopsy data.

claim: The model parameters may serve as early and robust biomarkers of the efficacy of checkpoint inhibitor therapy on an individualized per-patient basis.
source: Together, these suggest that the model parameters may serve as early and robust biomarkers of the efficacy of checkpoint inhibitor therapy on an individualized per-patient basis.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the model's predictive performance and biological validation.

claim: Checkpoint inhibitor therapy has led to markedly improved survival in the setting of previously intractable metastatic melanoma, bladder, kidney, lung, and head and neck cancers.
source: Recent advances in the understanding of immunological pathways responsible for antibody- and/or cell-mediated destruction of tumors have led to the development of unique cancer therapeutics in recent years, leading to markedly improved survival in the setting of previously intractable metastatic melanoma, bladder, kidney, lung, and head and neck cancers, among several other human solid tumor types (Borghaei et al., 2015; Robert et al., 2015a; Robert et al., 2015b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published clinical trials.

claim: Antibodies directed against the programmed death protein 1 (PD-1) pathway inhibit cellular immune killing of cancer cells via complementary binding of tumor expressed programmed death ligand 1 (PD-L1) to PD-1 on immune cells.
source: In particular, one of the most successful clinical applications of immune checkpoint inhibitors includes antibodies directed against the programmed death protein 1 (PD-1) pathway, which inhibits cellular immune killing of cancer cells via complementary binding of tumor expressed programmed death ligand 1 (PD-L1) to PD-1 on immune cells (Pardoll, 2012).
evidence: This describes the biological mechanism of PD-1/PD-L1 checkpoint inhibition, supported by citation.

claim: Targeting of immune checkpoints is being extensively investigated in ongoing and upcoming clinical trials aimed at unleashing T cell activity, augmenting immune recognition against tumor metastases, and boosting immune memory for long-lasting clinical remission post-treatment.
source: As a still emerging yet quite compelling immunotherapy approach in contemporary cancer medicine, targeting of immune checkpoints is being extensively investigated in ongoing and upcoming clinical trials aimed at unleashing T cell activity, augmenting immune recognition against tumor metastases, and boosting immune memory for long-lasting clinical remission post-treatment (Postow et al., 2015; Le et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes the current state of clinical research in checkpoint inhibitor therapy, supported by citations.

claim: Durable effective treatment outcomes with checkpoint inhibitors occur only in a limited subset of patients.
source: While the remarkable potential for checkpoint inhibitors in treating cancer is unequivocally exciting, the combined clinical trial experience has shown that durable effective treatment outcomes occur only in a limited subset of patients (Sharma et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a summary of clinical trial outcomes, supported by citation.

claim: Some cancer types are presumed to be minimally immunogenic, resulting in little or no response to checkpoint inhibitor treatment.
source: Alas, some cancer types are presumed to be minimally immunogenic, resulting in little or no response to this treatment strategy (Brahmer et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a statement about cancer immunogenicity and treatment response, supported by citation.

claim: Certain immunological features, including T cell exhaustion (e.g., Tim-3) and exclusion, could reflect or predict sensitivity and resistance to checkpoint inhibitor-based cancer immunotherapy.
source: An accumulating body of evidence has established that certain immunological features, including T cell exhaustion (e.g., Tim-3) and exclusion (Jerby-Arnon et al., 2018), senescence markers (Moreira et al., 2019) such as CD57, or immune incompetence, exhaustion, or premature senescence (e.g., loss of CD27) (Riaz et al., 2017; Vallejo, 2005), could perhaps reflect or even predict sensitivity and resistance to checkpoint inhibitor-based cancer immunotherapy.
evidence: This summarizes evidence from multiple studies about immunological biomarkers, supported by citations.

claim: Early attempts at identification of specific pathological biomarkers to predict immunotherapy response have shown somewhat inconsistent results.
source: However, early attempts at identification of specific pathological biomarkers to predict immunotherapy response, including transcriptomic rubrics (Auslander et al., 2018), machine learning algorithms (Johannet et al., 2021), genomic approaches (Cormedi et al., 2021) such as tumor mutational burden (Duffy and Crown, 2019), among others (Pilard et al., 2021), have thus far shown somewhat inconsistent results, challenged further by the inherent molecular, cellular, and biophysical diversity of human tumors (Teng et al., 2015; Tumeh et al., 2014; Carbognin et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a summary of the current state of biomarker research, supported by multiple citations.

claim: Most currently applied parameters merely document tumor responses that have already occurred as opposed to predicting it a priori.
source: Instead, most currently applied parameters merely document tumor responses that have already occurred as opposed to predicting it a priori; these include the standard Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumor (RECIST) v1.1 (Eisenhauer et al., 2009) and even the newer proposed response assessment rubrics specific for immunotherapy (iRECIST).
evidence: This is a critique of current clinical assessment methods, supported by citation.

claim: Mechanistic mathematical models of immunomodulatory interventions for cancer control have allowed the prediction of tumor response after Bacillus Calmette–Guérin (BCG) administration in superficial transitional cell carcinoma of the urinary bladder with considerable accuracy.
source: In previous work, mechanistic mathematical models of immunomodulatory interventions for cancer control utilizing coupled ordinary differential equations (ODEs) have already allowed the prediction of tumor response after Bacillus Calmette–Guérin (BCG) administration in superficial transitional cell carcinoma of the urinary bladder and the serum prostate-specific antigen response after prostate cancer vaccine administration with considerable accuracy (Bunimovich-Mendrazitsky et al., 2016; Bunimovich-Mendrazitsky et al., 2007; Kronik et al., 2010).
evidence: This describes prior work in mathematical modeling of cancer immunotherapy, supported by citations.

claim: Mechanistic models of interleukin-21 (IL-21) therapy schedules based on tumor mass and antigenic properties can predict growth patterns of multiple tumor types in patients receiving personalized doses of IL-21.
source: Moreover, other investigators have shown that mechanistic models of interleukin-21 (IL-21) therapy schedules based on tumor mass and antigenic properties can predict growth patterns of multiple tumor types in patients receiving personalized doses of IL-21 (de Pillis et al., 2005).
evidence: This describes prior modeling work, supported by citation.

claim: Mathematical modeling of neoantigen fitness based on cancer population evolution and antigen recognition potential was able to predict tumor response and patient survival following treatment with checkpoint blockade therapy in melanoma patients treated with anti-CTLA4 and in lung cancer patients treated with anti-PD-1 therapies.
source: In another notable work, mathematical modeling of neoantigen fitness based on cancer population evolution and antigen recognition potential was able to predict tumor response and patient survival following treatment with checkpoint blockade therapy, as validated in both melanoma patients treated with anti-CTLA4 and in lung cancer patients treated with anti-PD-1 therapies (Łuksza et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes prior modeling work in checkpoint inhibitor therapy, supported by citation.

claim: Modeling of chemotherapy and targeted drug therapy was able to accurately reproduce entire dose–response curves of tumor cell kill with untargeted cytotoxic and ligand-directed agents.
source: Finally, modeling of chemotherapy and targeted drug therapy by our group with similar mathematical techniques was able to accurately reproduce entire dose–response curves of tumor cell kill with untargeted cytotoxic and ligand-directed agents (Pascal et al., 2013a; Hosoya et al., 2016; Dogra et al., 2018; Goel et al., 2019; Dogra et al., 2020b).
evidence: This describes prior work by the authors' group, supported by citations.

claim: The final mathematical model used for comparison with clinical data is a single ordinary differential equation (ODE), which determines changes in relative tumor mass over time after initiation of anti-PD-1 therapy.
source: The final mathematical model we used for comparison with clinical data is a single ODE, which determines changes in relative tumor mass over time after initiation of anti-PD-1 therapy.
evidence: This describes the structure of the mathematical model.

claim: The model is a simplified and user-friendly version originated from a complex set of partial differential equations (PDEs), which takes into account spatial relationships within the tumor microenvironment.
source: It is a simplified and user-friendly version originated from a complex set of partial differential equations (PDEs), which takes into account spatial relationships within the tumor microenvironment.
evidence: This describes the derivation of the model from more complex equations.

claim: The model assumes tumor mass grows exponentially with rate α in the absence of immune cell killing.
source: Equation (1) assumes the following five assumptions: (i) tumor mass grows exponentially with rate α in the absence of immune cell killing
evidence: This is an explicit assumption of the mathematical model.

claim: The model assumes the influx of immune cells and the concentration of checkpoint inhibitor within the tumor environment reaches a drug steady state on time scales far faster (from hours to days) than clinical response (from weeks to months).
source: (iii) the influx of immune cells and the concentration of checkpoint inhibitor within the tumor environment reaches a drug steady state on time scales far faster (i.e., from hours to days) than clinical response (i.e., from weeks to months)
evidence: This is an explicit assumption of the mathematical model.

claim: The model assumes all cancer cells are within an average intratumoral movement path length of effector immune cells, and the effect of cytokines in stimulating immune cell function/movement is small, thus spatial diversity effects are negligible.
source: (iv) all cancer cells are within an average intratumoral movement path length of effector immune cells, and the effect of cytokines in stimulating immune cell function/movement is small, thus spatial diversity effects are negligible in this particular case
evidence: This is an explicit assumption of the mathematical model.

claim: The model assumes the site of action of the checkpoint inhibitor takes place at the interface between the tumor cell and immune cell, with blocking of one of the immune checkpoint receptors necessary and sufficient for blockade of the immune inhibitory pathway.
source: (v) the site of action of the checkpoint inhibitor takes place at the interface between the tumor cell and immune cell, with blocking of one of the immune checkpoint receptors, either on the cancer or on the immune cell, which are deemed necessary and sufficient for blockade of the immune inhibitory pathway.
evidence: This is an explicit assumption of the mathematical model.

claim: Tumor volumes over time measurements were obtained from six published clinical trial reports.
source: To evaluate Equation (1) with clinical data, we initially focused on clinical trials with the class of checkpoint inhibitors that specifically target the PD-1/PD-L1 pathway. In this analysis, tumor volumes over time measurements were obtained from six published clinical trial reports (Borghaei et al., 2015; Antonia et al., 2015; Le et al., 2015; Motzer et al., 2015; Powles et al., 2014; Topalian et al., 2012).
evidence: This describes the data sources used for model calibration.

claim: The combined dataset from six clinical trials represents 189 cancer patients.
source: As an initial retrospective proof of concept, five clinical trials of anti-PD-1 therapy plus another clinical trial of anti-PD-L1 treatment (Table 1) were included, with the combined dataset representing several common solid tumor pathology types (n = 189 cancer patients); this dataset represents our model calibration cohort.
evidence: This describes the size of the calibration cohort.

claim: Of the 189 patients in the calibration cohort, 55 patients (29%) had objective responses by RECIST v1.1 criteria while 134 patients (71%) demonstrated stable/progressive disease.
source: Of this population, 55 patients (29%) had objective responses by RECIST v1.1 criteria while 134 patients (71%) demonstrated stable/progressive disease.
evidence: This is a quantitative description of the patient outcomes in the calibration cohort.

claim: The derived tumor proliferation constant, α, ranged from 0.0034 (tumor doubling time of ~200 days) in renal cell carcinoma to 0.0622 (tumor doubling time of ~11 days) in non-mismatch repair colon cancer.
source: The derived tumor proliferation constant, α, was determined to range from 0.0034 (tumor doubling time of ~200 days) in renal cell carcinoma to 0.0622 (tumor doubling time of ~11 days) in non-mismatch repair colon cancer with an average α of 0.018 and average tumor doubling time of ~85 days (Table 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from fitting the model to clinical data.

claim: The average α was 0.018 with an average tumor doubling time of ~85 days.
source: The derived tumor proliferation constant, α, was determined to range from 0.0034 (tumor doubling time of ~200 days) in renal cell carcinoma to 0.0622 (tumor doubling time of ~11 days) in non-mismatch repair colon cancer with an average α of 0.018 and average tumor doubling time of ~85 days (Table 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from fitting the model to clinical data.

claim: In the validation NSCLC cohort, 25 patients (39%) had objective response, and 39 patients (61%) demonstrated stable/progressive disease.
source: In the validation NSCLC cohort, 25 patients (39%) had objective response, and 39 patients (61%) demonstrated stable/progressive disease, with individual patient proliferation constants (α) ranging from –0.0129 to 0.0602 (note that α < 0 indicates a subset of patients that had a shrinking tumor burden before start of therapy).

claim: In the validation NSCLC cohort, individual patient proliferation constants (α) ranged from –0.0129 to 0.0602.
source: In the validation NSCLC cohort, 25 patients (39%) had objective response, and 39 patients (61%) demonstrated stable/progressive disease, with individual patient proliferation constants (α) ranging from –0.0129 to 0.0602 (note that α < 0 indicates a subset of patients that had a shrinking tumor burden before start of therapy).

source: The average root-mean-square error of fitting Equation (1) to the clinical data was only 0.4%.

source: The derived fits from all 189 patient response curves in the calibration cohort yielded a mean ± standard error of the mean (SEM) value of Λ of 0.714 ± 0.257 in patients with partial/complete response and 0.0995 ± 0.0264 in patients with stable/progressive disease (p=0.119; Wilcoxon two-tail)
evidence: This is a quantitative statistical result from the calibration cohort.

source: while the mean ± SEM value of µ was 0.054 ± 0.014 versus 0.013 ± 0.0012 in partial/complete response versus stable/progressive disease, respectively (p<0.001).

source: In the validation NSCLC cohort, the mean ± SEM value of Λ was 0.876 ± 0.102 in patients with partial/complete response and 0.0297 ± 0.469 in patients with stable/progressive disease (p<0.001)

source: while Spearman correlation coefficients for µ ranged from 0.910 (t < 30 days) to 0.921 (t < 200 days) for all truncated datasets (Table 2).

source: Simulated RECIST v1.1 categorization (complete/partial response vs. stable/progressive disease) by using the values of Λ and µ derived from fitting the truncated calibration cohort data resulted in 19% misclassification by using data from t < 60 days (n = 177) and 13% misclassification at t < 200 days (n = 189) when compared to the full dataset.
evidence: This is a result from the predictive performance analysis using truncated data.

claim: In the validation cohort, 18.6% misclassification was observed at t < 60 days and 10.9% misclassification at t <200 days.
source: In the validation cohort, we observed 18.6% misclassification at t < 60 days (n = 43) and 10.9% misclassification at t <200 days (n = 64).
evidence: This is a result from the predictive performance analysis in the validation cohort.

claim: Conversion of Λ to an estimated intratumoral CD8+ T cell count yielded a predicted mean ± SEM of 3970 ± 1429 cells/mm2 in patients with partial/complete response to checkpoint inhibition and 553 ± 147 cells/mm2 in patients with stable/progressive disease in the calibration cohort.
source: Conversion of Λ to an estimated intratumoral CD8+ T cell count yielded a predicted mean ± SEM of 3970 ± 1429 cells/mm2 in patients with partial/complete response to checkpoint inhibition and 553 ± 147 cells/mm2 in patients with stable/progressive disease (Figure 5) in the calibration cohort
evidence: This is a result from converting the model parameter Λ to a biological measure, shown in Figure 5.

source: In the pretreatment setting, the average intratumoral CD8+ T cell count was 2632 ± 518 cells/mm2 in patients with partial/complete response to checkpoint inhibitors and 322 ± 133 cells/mm2 in patients demonstrating stable/progressive disease

source: while in the validation cohort, the model-predicted ORR was 9% and 71% for patients with µ < 1% and ≥1%, respectively

claim: The mathematical model is fully compatible with the current understanding of the biological effect of checkpoint blockade and clinical subtypes of immunotherapy-responsive tumors.
source: From a mechanistic standpoint, the mathematical model is fully compatible with the current understanding of the biological effect of checkpoint blockade and clinical subtypes of immunotherapy-responsive tumors (Teng et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a statement about the biological validity of the model, supported by citation.

claim: The parameter values derived from the model for intratumoral immune cell infiltration (Λ) and immunotherapy antibody efficacy (µ) correspond with the quantitative pathological measures of intratumoral CD8+ T cell infiltration and PD-L1-positive staining.
source: First, the parameter values derived from our model for intratumoral immune cell infiltration (Λ) and immunotherapy antibody efficacy (µ) correspond with the quantitative pathological measures of intratumoral CD8+ T cell infiltration and PD-L1-positive staining (Figure 4; Figure 5).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of model parameters with biological measurements, shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: The model demonstrates that the rate of immunotherapy response arises from nonlinear interactions between both adequate effector immune cell infiltration in tumors and immunotherapy efficacy within the tumor microenvironment.
source: Moreover, the model demonstrates that the rate of immunotherapy response arises from nonlinear interactions between both adequate effector immune cell infiltration in tumors and immunotherapy efficacy within the tumor microenvironment (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the model structure and results, shown in Figure 4.

claim: Mechanistic mathematical modeling across several cancer types suggests that the overlying master equation may be universally applied, while the model parameter values are likely tumor-specific.
source: Mechanistic mathematical modeling across several cancer types (Table 1) suggests that the overlying master equation [i.e., Equation (1)] may well be universally applied, while the model parameter values presented here are likely tumor-specific.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the model's performance across multiple cancer types.

claim: The high sensitivity at early time points (t < 60 days) indicates that this model may provide valuable early identification of cancer patients most likely to benefit from checkpoint inhibition therapy.
source: The high sensitivity at early time points (t < 60 days) demonstrated here indicates that this model may provide valuable early identification of cancer patients most likely to benefit from checkpoint inhibition therapy, with a high NPV indicating minimal false-negatives in the group predicted to receive the least benefit from therapy.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the model's predictive performance at early time points.

claim: A mathematical model with two simple terms (an exponential growth term and a regression term) has previously been used to successfully correlate and predict patient survival.
source: Towards clinical translation of cancer models, a mathematical model with two simple terms (an exponential growth term and a regression term) has previously been used to successfully correlate and predict patient survival (Stein et al., 2008).
evidence: This describes prior work in mathematical modeling of cancer, supported by citation.

claim: The fundamental difference between the prior model by Stein et al., 2008 and the model reported here is that the quantification of cell death is more mechanistic, depending on specific mechanisms that underlie cancer cell and immunotherapy drug interactions.
source: The fundamental difference between this prior model (Stein et al., 2008) and the model reported here is that the quantification of cell death is more mechanistic, that is, depending on the specific mechanisms (Figure 1) that underlie cancer cell and immunotherapy drug interactions, hence allowing one to gain more mechanistic insight into the treatment system.
evidence: This is a comparison between the current model and prior work, referencing Figure 1.

claim: Model parameters Λ and µ can be used to stratify responding and nonresponding patients.
source: As demonstrated, model parameters Λ and µ can be used to stratify responding and nonresponding patients (Figure 3), which has immediate potential utility as a biomarker for patient selection in prospective clinical trials.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the results shown in Figure 3.

claim: The model may be informed by using standard-of-care measurements.
source: Thus, we expect that the model (i) may be informed by using standard-of-care measurements (e.g., Figure 5)
evidence: This is a conclusion about the clinical applicability of the model, referencing Figure 5.

claim: The model can provide quantitative information on which parameters must be changed to maximize therapeutic benefit, providing clinicians with potentially valuable decision-making information.
source: and (ii) can provide quantitative information on which parameters must be changed to maximize therapeutic benefit, providing clinicians with potentially valuable decision-making information.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the potential clinical utility of the model.

claim: The model does not explicitly include the presence of immunosuppressive cells (such as neutrophils, myeloid-derived suppressor cells, Treg, and M2-polarized tumor-associated macrophages), which extensively infiltrate into tumor mass and hinder the efficacy of immune checkpoint inhibitors.
source: These include the presence of immunosuppressive cells (such as neutrophils, myeloid-derived suppressor cells, Treg, and M2-polarized tumor-associated macrophages), which extensively infiltrate into tumor mass and hinder the efficacy of immune checkpoint inhibitors (Jenkins et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a limitation of the model acknowledged by the authors, supported by citation.

claim: Effects of other immune cells, such as CD4+ T cells, are not explicitly included in the current model form.
source: Moreover, effects of other immune cells, such as CD4+ T cells, are not explicitly included in the current model form; while it is likely that some of the effects from these other cells are captured within the model representation of CD8+ T cells, this assumption warrants future model development where each immune component is explicitly represented.
evidence: This is a limitation of the model acknowledged by the authors.

claim: High rates of immune cell binding by anti-PD1 antibodies occur in the peripheral circulation.
source: Some of these assumptions (e.g., lack of immune cell/antibody infiltration terms) are supported with in vitro or in vivo data such as high rates of immune cell binding by anti-PD1 antibodies in the peripheral circulation (Topalian et al., 2012)
evidence: This is a biological observation supporting one of the model assumptions, supported by citation.

claim: Local intratumoral (as opposed to systemic myelogenous) expansion of CD8+ T cells occurs during checkpoint inhibition.
source: and local intratumoral (as opposed to systemic myelogenous) expansion of CD8+ T cells during checkpoint inhibition (Tumeh et al., 2014; Ribas et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a biological observation supporting one of the model assumptions, supported by citations.

claim: Response was defined using RECIST v1.1 criteria, in lieu of the more recent adaptation of RECIST criteria to immunotherapy treatment (iRECIST), because the studies used to derive the model parameters did not incorporate these new criteria.
source: Response was defined using RECIST v1.1 criteria, in lieu of the more recent adaptation of RECIST criteria to immunotherapy treatment (iRECIST), because the studies used to derive the model parameters in this mechanistic analysis did not incorporate these new criteria, and our use of published data for the calibration cohort limited or precluded us from obtaining a priori knowledge about nontarget lesions.
